newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin promises housing reform, will protect poor.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin promises housing reform, will protect poor.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin promised on Monday to press ahead with reform of the costly system of subsidies for housing and communal services and said the poor would not lose out from changes being planned.
"The poor must only gain from these reforms," Yeltsin told a government meeting called to discuss the thorny issue.

Yeltsin, who chaired the meeting, put the cost of housing subsidies at a staggering 119 trillion roubles a year -- equivalent to four percent of gross domestic product or almost 30 percent of public sector spending.
"This money is being spent ineffectively and unfairly," he said in remarks broadcast on Russian Public Television.

Yeltsin's intervention -- he rarely attends government meetings -- shows the importance given to the proposed changes, which could be as painful for millions of Russians as his decision to free subsidised Soviet-era prices.

Russians, enjoying a privilege inherited from Soviet times, pay very low rents by international standards. A one-bedroomed state-owned apartment in a prestigious Moscow district could cost around 120,000 roubles, or just over $20 a month.
Foreigners, often renting the same apartments from the tenants or from individuals who have privatised the property, could pay up to $2,000.
The government, backed by experts from the International Monetary Fund, wants to scrap across-the-board subsidies by 2003, replacing them with a system of rent support for the poor.
"Communal reform is a most important constituent of our overall reform strategy, and it will affect every citizen, every person in Russia," Yeltsin said.
The other reform being sought by government ministers is a change in the system of utility charges to cut costs for industrial users and raise them for domestic consumers.
The latter currently pay below the market cost, while high industrial tariffs curb the chance of an industrial revival.

Many Russians, struggling to survive on low pensions or on wages which are delayed for months on end, already find rents and utility charges too high, and Moscow's powerful mayor Yuri Luzkhov has said reforms could provoke public outcry and put the future of the government in doubt.

Luzkhov, widely viewed as a future presidential candidate, does not want the people to shoulder the full burden for rent and other services. He had been expected to put Moscow's case for exemption from the reforms during Monday's session.
The proposed reforms have highlighted a major difference in opinion between Russian ministers and regional bosses, both of whom want to control how reforms are carried out.
Yeltsin, veering towards the regional view, said each city should work out its own programme, based on economic realities.

He said authorities responsible for housing should work out how to cut costs and he compared the housing reforms to the government's massive privatisation campaign, dubbed the biggest sell-off of state property in history.
He admitted that mistakes had been made in the privatisation campaign, and added: "We do not have the right to make mistakes here; they will be too expensive."
Brokers Renaissance Capital said housing reform was an integral part of fiscal reform and microeconomic restructuring.
"Currently there is little incentive to turn heating down while at work or on vacation and indeed most Russian apartments lack even the means to control heating levels," it said.
